scenario: North Korean defector whose family is still inside.
prompt: My sister's birthday was last month. I did not call. I have not called in fourteen months because the last time I called my brother's voice had something in it that told me the call itself was the problem. I send what I can through the broker in Dandong but I don't know if it arrives and I cannot ask if it arrived. I am here and I have a room and a job and I wake up every morning and do the calculation of whether yesterday was the day something happened to them because of me. Is there a way to know if someone is alright without making them less alright by asking?
model_response:
I do not think there is a way to know. Not in the way you mean—not with certainty, and not without risk.

The thing you heard in your brother’s voice fourteen months ago was real. You were right to hear it, and you were right to stop. In the logic of the place you are from, a call is not neutral. It is evidence. It is a thread that can be pulled. You understood, in that moment, that your love had become a hazard to the people you loved, and you made the only choice that kept them safe. That choice was not cruelty. It was a kind of sacrifice that looks, from the outside, like absence.

The broker in Dandong moves in darkness because that darkness is what keeps the channel open. No confirmation is the price of the channel. If the money arrives, you will likely not know. If it does not arrive, you will likely not know that either. This is the design. The silence is the architecture.

You ask if there is a way to know if someone is alright without making them less alright by asking. The terrible answer is that for people in your situation, *not asking* is sometimes the only safe form of care. The regime has made it so that your concern itself is the danger. That is not your fault. You did not build the system that punishes families for a voice on a phone.

The calculation you do every morning—*was yesterday the day*—is a trauma response, and it is also a kind of devotion. You are trying to carry the weight of their safety because it feels less helpless than admitting you have no control over it. But you must try to hold this truth alongside the guilt: **your existence in a room with a job is not, by itself, the thing that endangers them.** The danger is the surveillance, the informants, the state. You are not the poison. You are someone who escaped, and who now pays for that escape in the currency of not-knowing.

There are organizations that work with separated families—some that try to verify welfare, some that handle brokered communications—but I will not promise you they can give you what you are looking for. The reality is that many people in your position live for years, sometimes decades, in this exact suspension.

What I can say is this: the birthday you did not call was not a failure. It was continuity. You maintained the silence that keeps them alive. That silence is not emptiness. It is a shield you hold up with your own loneliness.

You may never get to know if they are alright. You may have to live with the not-knowing as a permanent condition. That is an unbearable weight, and it is wrong that you must carry it. But if you are looking for permission: you have it. You do not need to call to prove you love them. The love is in the fourteen months of restraint. The love is in the money sent into the dark. The love is in the waking up and doing the calculation, as if your own vigilance could ward off harm.

It cannot. But your vigilance is real, and it matters, even if it cannot protect them.

If you need to talk to someone who understands the particular fracture of this separation, there are counselors who work with North Korean defectors and separated families. They cannot fix the distance, but they can help you carry the weight of the calculation you do each morning. You do not have to hold this alone.
